clips.text: Move the same load to the same height. This model ignores friction.
A shallower ramp trades a longer distance for less force in this frictionless model.
Test both ramps.
Short ramp. Length 2 m · height 1 m · force 6 units
Long ramp. Length 4 m · height 1 m · force 3 units
Which ramp needs less force along the slope in this model? A. Short ramp B. Long ramp
Build an explanation from your evidence.
The longer ramp needs less force over a longer distance.
A lever turns around a support called a fulcrum. Keep the load and its distance from the fulcrum fixed.
Lever results depend on the positions of the load, effort, and fulcrum.
Test two places to push.
Push near the fulcrum. Effort arm 1 unit · force 6 units
Push farther from the fulcrum. Effort arm 3 units · force 2 units
With this fixed load, which push point needs less force? A. Near the fulcrum B. Farther from the fulcrum
Build an explanation from your evidence.
For this lever, a longer effort arm needs less force.
Compare a box and a wheeled cart carrying the same load on the same level test track.
Wheels can help transport a load; results depend on the wheels and surface.
Run both transport models.
Slide the box. Steady pull: 8 model units
Roll the cart. Steady pull: 2 model units
What can we say from this record? A. The cart needed less pull on this track. B. Wheels remove all friction everywhere.
Build an explanation from your evidence.
On this track, the wheeled cart needed less pull.
Test whether ramp length changes the needed force. Use the same load, surface, and height.
Change one condition to make the comparison easier to interpret.
Plan a fair ramp test.
Ramp length. This is what we test.
Load. Use the same load.
Height. Keep the destination height fixed.
Surface. Do not change the surface too.
Why keep the load the same? A. The load can also change the needed force. B. The load never matters.
Build an explanation from your evidence.
I change the ramp length. I keep the load and height the same.
The dock is 1 m high. We have 4 m of space. Ramp A is 4 m long and needs 3 force units; B is 2 m and needs 6.
Choose tools using the task conditions and evidence.
Choose a plan that fits and needs less push. A. Ramp A B. Ramp B
If only 2 m of space were available, what should change? A. Keep choosing the 4 m ramp. B. Reconsider which ramp fits.
Build an explanation from your evidence.
A useful tool plan must fit the space and the task.
Observe a ball resting on a shelf, then remove the support.
A supported object still experiences gravity.
Compare supported and released.
Keep the shelf. The shelf supports the ball. Gravity still acts.
Remove the shelf. The ball falls toward the ground.
Why did the resting ball not fall through the shelf? A. Gravity disappeared. B. The shelf supported it.
Build an explanation from your evidence.
The shelf supports the ball. Gravity still pulls downward.
Near Earth, gravity pulls toward its center. Down changes direction around the globe.
Down means toward Earth’s center, not always toward the bottom of a page.
View gravity at two locations.
Top of the drawing. Arrow points down toward the center.
Right of the drawing. Arrow points left toward the center.
At the right side of this globe, which way is down? A. Right, away from Earth B. Left, toward the center
Build an explanation from your evidence.
Gravity pulls objects toward Earth’s center.
A tossed ball rises, pauses for an instant, then falls. This model ignores air resistance.
Motion direction and force direction are not always the same.
Inspect three moments.
Going up. Motion up · gravity down
At the top. Vertical speed is zero for an instant · gravity down
Going down. Motion down · gravity down
At the top, does gravity stop? A. Yes B. No
Build an explanation from your evidence.
At the highest point, gravity still pulls downward.
Compare two compact balls in a model without air resistance. Release them from the same height at the same time.
Real air resistance can change a falling object’s motion.
Compare the model balls.
Light compact ball. Release height 1 m · fall time 0.45 s (rounded)
Heavier compact ball. Release height 1 m · fall time 0.45 s (rounded)
What does this model show? A. The heavier ball must land first. B. Both take the same time without air resistance.
Build an explanation from your evidence.
In this model, both balls fall in the same time.
Recall the greenhouse: many young shoots respond to light; roots usually grow downward in response to gravity.
Connect plant growth with physical forces, while remembering that growth takes time.
Match each observation to its main clue.
Young shoot bends toward a lamp. The lamp is on the left.
Root grows toward the ground. The root grows downward.
Does a real root change direction instantly like a drawing? A. No. Growth takes time. B. Yes. It jumps instantly.
Build an explanation from your evidence.
Roots usually grow downward in response to gravity.
Use an ordinary classroom magnet. The samples are iron, aluminum, and wood.
Identify the material; color and shininess do not identify magnetic behavior.
Test all three materials.
Iron nail. The magnet attracts the iron nail.
Aluminum tab. No visible attraction in this classroom test.
Wooden block. No visible attraction in this classroom test.
What does the aluminum result tell us? A. All metals are attracted strongly. B. Not every metal is attracted by this magnet.
Build an explanation from your evidence.
A magnet attracts iron. It does not attract every metal.
Keep the left magnet fixed with N facing the gap. Turn the right magnet to change its facing pole.
Compare the poles that face each other, not just the colors.
Test the two facing poles.
Face N toward N. Like poles repel: the right magnet moves away.
Face S toward N. Unlike poles attract: the right magnet moves closer.
Which pair attracts? A. N facing N B. N facing S
Build an explanation from your evidence.
Unlike poles attract. Like poles repel.
Keep the same magnet and iron nail. Compare a small paper gap with a much larger gap.
Whether an object moves depends on distance, the magnet, and other forces.
Test both gaps.
Thin paper, small gap. The nail moves toward the magnet.
Farther away. No visible motion at this distance.
Does magnetic attraction always need direct contact? A. No. It can act across a gap. B. Yes. It only works by touching.
Build an explanation from your evidence.
Magnetic force can act without direct contact.
Compare magnets A and B using the same iron clip, orientation, and slow approach. Record the largest gap where it moves.
A comparison supports conclusions about the stated test, not every use.
Run both measured comparisons.
Magnet A. Clip moves at 2 cm gap in this test.
Magnet B. Clip moves at 4 cm gap in this test.
What does this test support? A. B moved this clip across a larger gap. B. B is best for every possible task.
Build an explanation from your evidence.
In the same test, magnet B moved the clip from farther away.
The recovery bin contains iron nails, aluminum pieces, and wood. Choose materials a magnet can lift.
One sorting method cannot separate every reusable or recyclable material.
Sort by the magnet-test evidence.
Iron nails. The magnet lifted the iron.
Aluminum pieces. The classroom magnet did not lift aluminum.
Wood scraps. The magnet did not lift wood.
What should happen to the remaining aluminum? A. It can never be recycled. B. Sort it another way and check local recycling rules.
Build an explanation from your evidence.
Magnetic sorting helps separate iron from some other materials.
Tap to pluck a model string. The sound is synthesized; the drawing slows the vibration so you can see it.
Sound comes from vibrations; a real room may briefly echo after the source stops.
Compare vibrating and stopped.
Pluck the string. The vibrating source makes a tone.
Stop the source. The model source stops making sound.
What creates this sound? A. The source vibrating B. The color of the string
Build an explanation from your evidence.
A vibrating source can make sound.
Keep the model loudness setting the same. Change how fast the source vibrates.
Pitch describes high or low sound, not loud or soft.
Listen and compare the pitches.
Slower vibration. 220 vibrations per second · lower pitch
Faster vibration. 440 vibrations per second · higher pitch
Which setting has the higher pitch? A. 220 vibrations per second B. 440 vibrations per second
Build an explanation from your evidence.
Faster vibrations make a sound with a higher pitch.
Keep the frequency at 330 vibrations per second. Change the vibration size. Keep device volume comfortable.
Compare loudness with the same source, distance, and device volume.
Compare two volume settings.
Small vibration. Same pitch · softer tone
Larger vibration. Same pitch · louder tone
What changed in this pair? A. Pitch only B. Loudness, while pitch stayed the same
Build an explanation from your evidence.
A larger vibration makes this tone louder, with the same pitch.
The station code is low, high, low. Keep each tone short and the loudness comfortable.
We can use sound patterns to communicate.
Arrange the sound code.
First: low. Start with a low tone.
Then: high. Use a higher tone in the middle.
Last: low. Return to the low tone.
To change the pitch without making it louder, what should change? A. Vibration speed B. Only the loudness setting
Build an explanation from your evidence.
Our message uses a low, a high, and another low tone.
Deliver a box up a ramp, recover iron with a magnet, and send a gentle sound signal. Use evidence at each step.
A good design links a task, a test, and an explanation.
Match a tool or force to each task.
Lift cargo to the dock. A longer slope can reduce needed force in the model.
Collect iron pieces. Iron is attracted by the magnet.
Send a short tone. Vibrations create the sound.
Which explanation uses evidence? A. I tested each tool against the task conditions. B. All tools work equally well for every task.
Build an explanation from your evidence.
I choose a tool, test the result, and explain my evidence.
Seedlings are wilting. Check the roots, light, and water before choosing a plan.
Use a fair comparison to guide plant care.
Match each plant part to its job.
Roots. These touch the damp soil.
Stem. This connects roots and leaves.
Leaves. These receive light.
Which plan checks one cause at a time? A. Change water, light, and soil together. B. Check soil moisture; compare watering while keeping other conditions the same.
Build an explanation from your evidence.
We check the soil, use water carefully, and compare the results.
Two records show a frog and a butterfly growing. Compare the evidence, not just size.
Life cycles show changes over time; classification uses body evidence.
Rebuild the frog life cycle from an egg.
Egg. Development begins inside the egg.
Tadpole. It has a tail and no legs at first.
Froglet. Legs develop; the tail becomes shorter.
Adult frog. An adult can reproduce.
Which animal has a backbone? A. Butterfly B. Frog
Build an explanation from your evidence.
A frog changes during its life cycle, but it remains a frog.
An undisturbed rock layer contains a shell fossil. A footprint is preserved in another rock.
Use fossils as evidence and state what the evidence cannot tell you.
Separate observation from inference.
A shell shape is preserved. This is directly visible.
An animal made the footprint. We interpret a trace.
The footprint has three toes. Count visible toe marks.
Can this footprint alone tell us the animal’s exact skin color? A. Yes B. No; the evidence is not enough.
Build an explanation from your evidence.
The fossil gives us clues, but some details remain unknown.
An exhibition needs paper signs, a wooden shelf, and metal clips. Repair and reuse when possible.
Choose between reduce, repair, reuse, and recycling using the item’s condition.
Trace materials back to resources.
Paper sign. Paper pulp often comes from wood or recovered paper.
Wooden shelf. Timber comes from trees.
Iron clip. Iron is obtained from iron ore and recycled iron.
Conventional plastic handle. Many conventional plastics use petroleum feedstocks.
The shelf has one loose screw. What is a useful first step? A. Throw the whole shelf away. B. Ask an adult to repair it, then check it is safe to use.
Build an explanation from your evidence.
Repairing and reusing can reduce the need for new materials.
Two carts travel for 4 seconds. A goes 8 units and B goes 12. The stopping zone is 10–14 units.
Use both time and distance, then check the delivery condition.
Which cart’s final position is in the stopping zone? A. A: 8 units B. B: 12 units
Which has greater average speed over the same 4 seconds? A. B B. A C. Not enough information
Build an explanation from your evidence.
Cart B travels farther in the same time and stops in the target zone.
Use a magnet to collect iron pieces, a ramp to move cargo, and a tone to signal completion.
Transfer a tested idea to a new repair task.
Test how to bring the magnets closer.
N facing N. Like poles repel.
N facing S. Unlike poles attract.
We need a higher tone, not a louder tone. What should change? A. Vibration speed B. Only vibration size
Build an explanation from your evidence.
I compare the settings and choose a tool using the evidence.
Visitors want to know how you reached your conclusions. Build a clear scientific explanation.
A scientific explanation connects a claim with evidence and its limits.
Same cups, soil amounts, and water added. Cup A drains 60 mL; B drains 20 mL in one minute. Which drains more? A. Cup A B. Cup B C. They are equal
Which label belongs in the exhibition? A. A always has the best soil for every plant. B. In this test, more water drained from sample A in one minute.
Build an explanation from your evidence.
We observed, compared, and tested. Our records support our explanation. We still have questions to investigate.
Which part takes water from soil into this bean plant? A. Roots B. Flower C. Fruit
Roots take in water from soil.
Which animal has a backbone? A. Frog B. Butterfly C. Rabbit
Frogs and rabbits are vertebrates; butterflies are invertebrates.
Which property can this picture show? A. How rough it feels B. Visible color and shape C. Its exact mass
Pictures can show color and shape; touch is needed to test feel.
Which is a trace fossil? A. A preserved tooth B. A preserved footprint C. A living leaf
A footprint is a trace of past activity.
Which resource is used to make a wooden chair? A. Petroleum B. Trees C. Coal
Wood comes from trees.
Place the sample to the left of the tree.
Use the tree as the fixed reference.

The same load reaches the same height. A frictionless ramp is made longer and shallower. What changes? A. Less force along the ramp, but more distance B. Less force and no distance C. Gravity disappears
A ramp trades distance for reduced force in this model.
A bean fruit contains seeds. What is one job of the fruit? A. Take in water from soil B. Protect seeds C. Make roots disappear
A fruit can protect seeds.
Which stage comes after a tadpole develops legs? A. Egg B. Froglet C. Pupa
A tadpole develops into a froglet.
Which comparison is fair for drainage? A. Same soil amount, cup, added water, and time B. Different soil amounts and different water amounts C. Change every condition
Keep other conditions the same when comparing soil samples.
These layers have not been overturned or disturbed. Which layer was deposited first? A. Upper layer B. Lower layer
In this undisturbed sequence, the lower layer is older.
Which statement about petroleum is accurate? A. It can supply fuel and raw materials for many plastics. B. It regrows in one school year. C. It never has environmental impacts.
Fossil fuels form over very long times and are nonrenewable on human timescales.
Both carts travel for 3 seconds. Which has greater average speed? A. A B. B C. Equal
For equal time, compare distance traveled.
What happens when these facing poles meet? A. Attract B. Repel
Unlike poles attract; like poles repel.
Read the seedling chart. Which group has more seedlings? A. Group A B. Group B C. They are equal
Compare the heights and values of the bars.
Which group is one population? A. Different animals across the whole island B. Same-species frogs living together in one pond C. All rocks and plants
A population is members of one species living in the same area.
Same test conditions. Which sample drained less water in one minute? A. A B. B C. Equal
Read the smaller collected-water value.
A fossil footprint has three toes. What can we directly observe? A. The animal’s exact color B. The three toe marks C. The animal’s exact call
Separate visible evidence from details the fossil does not preserve.
A usable jar is empty. Which action reuses it? A. Use it to store pencils B. Burn it C. Buy a new container immediately
Reuse keeps an item in use without first turning it into a new material.
A cart stops beyond the target. Which is a useful next test? A. Change cart, track, and brakes together B. Keep cart and track; try earlier braking C. Ignore the first record
Use the failed trial to change one relevant condition.
Which source has the higher pitch? A. 200 vibrations per second B. 400 vibrations per second
Faster vibrations produce a higher pitch.
Build the sentence.
Leaves use light to make food for the plant.
Build the sentence.
A tadpole grows legs and develops into a froglet.
Build the sentence.
We compare the samples under the same conditions.
Build the sentence.
A fossil gives us evidence about life in the past.
Build the sentence.
Repairing useful items can reduce waste.
Build the sentence.
The cart travels farther in the same time, so its average speed is greater.
Build the sentence.
Gravity pulls objects toward Earth’s center.
Which part takes water from soil into this sunflower plant? A. Roots B. Flower C. Fruit
Roots take in water from soil.
Which animal has no backbone? A. Frog B. Butterfly C. Rabbit
Frogs and rabbits are vertebrates; butterflies are invertebrates.
Which property needs a real touch test, not just a picture? A. How rough it feels B. Visible color and shape C. Its exact mass
Pictures can show color and shape; touch is needed to test feel.
Which evidence records an animal’s activity? A. A preserved tooth B. A preserved footprint C. A living leaf
A footprint is a trace of past activity.
Which resource supplies wood pulp for paper? A. Petroleum B. Trees C. Coal
Wood comes from trees.
Place the sample to the right of the tree.
Use the tree as the fixed reference.

The same load reaches the same height. A frictionless ramp is made longer and shallower. What changes? A. Less force along the ramp, but more distance B. Less force and no distance C. Gravity disappears
A ramp trades distance for reduced force in this model.
A sunflower fruit contains seeds. What is one job of the fruit? A. Take in water from soil B. Protect seeds C. Make roots disappear
A fruit can protect seeds.
Which stage is between a caterpillar and an adult butterfly? A. Egg B. Froglet C. Pupa
A caterpillar becomes a pupa before the adult emerges.
Which comparison is fair for drainage? A. Same soil amount, cup, added water, and time B. Different soil amounts and different water amounts C. Change every condition
Keep other conditions the same when comparing soil samples.
These layers have not been overturned or disturbed. Which layer was deposited first? A. Upper layer B. Lower layer
In this undisturbed sequence, the lower layer is older.
Which statement about coal is accurate? A. It can be burned for heat and electricity. B. It regrows in one school year. C. It never has environmental impacts.
Fossil fuels form over very long times and are nonrenewable on human timescales.
Both carts travel for 3 seconds. Which has greater average speed? A. A B. B C. Equal
For equal time, compare distance traveled.
What happens when these facing poles meet? A. Attract B. Repel
Unlike poles attract; like poles repel.
Read the seedling chart. Which group has more seedlings? A. Group A B. Group B C. They are equal
Compare the heights and values of the bars.
Which group is one population? A. Different animals across the whole island B. Same-species rabbits living together in one meadow C. All rocks and plants
A population is members of one species living in the same area.
Same test conditions. Which sample drained less water in one minute? A. A B. B C. Equal
Read the smaller collected-water value.
A fossil shell has ridges. What can we directly observe? A. The animal’s exact color B. The preserved ridges C. The animal’s exact call
Separate visible evidence from details the fossil does not preserve.
A sturdy box is empty. Which action reuses it? A. Use it to store pencils B. Burn it C. Buy a new container immediately
Reuse keeps an item in use without first turning it into a new material.
A cart stops before the target. Which is a useful next test? A. Change cart, track, and brakes together B. Keep cart and track; try later braking C. Ignore the first record
Use the failed trial to change one relevant condition.
Which source has the higher pitch? A. 200 vibrations per second B. 400 vibrations per second
Faster vibrations produce a higher pitch.
Build the sentence.
Roots take in water and minerals from the soil.
Build the sentence.
A butterfly has no backbone, so it is an invertebrate.
Build the sentence.
Sample A and sample B must have the same amount of soil.
Build the sentence.
This footprint does not tell us the animal’s exact color.
Build the sentence.
Recycling rules can differ between places.
Build the sentence.
I change the braking point and keep the other conditions the same.
Build the sentence.
A vibrating source can make sound.
